chapter: Los Angeles, Central Avenue and the Apex
title: A racially mixed Los Angeles and Jefferson High
summary: Remembering Los Angeles in 1918 as a mix of races and Jefferson High as roughly ten percent black, with Ralph Bunche as an alumnus.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: What do you remember about Los Angeles,

Growing up in Los Angeles. Well, I don't know. Los Angeles was quite a different place from what it is now. When I came up, my neighborhood was completely mixed up with just about a potpourri of every race that you could ever think about, because Los Angeles, when I came here, didn't have a lot of people in 1918. It was sort of like a oasis sitting out in this part of the world out here.

All of my friends that I went to school with were all mixed up races. There were many, many Jewish people, many Mexicans, a few Indians, Irish and Assyrians and there were Russians, just a whole mix-up of everything. The school that I went to, the high school that I went to at that time, had about ten percent blacks in it. That high school today is 100 percent black, Jefferson High School. It's the same school, as a matter of fact, that Ralph Bunch graduated from in the first graduation class, I think around 1916. I think he was in the first graduation class. Ralph Bunch was a pretty famous guy.
Jefferson had a lot of illustrious alumni, hasn't it?

Oh, yes. A lot of people up there that stood for something. It seemed like everyone tried just a little bit harder in those days because they had everything to gain. Children as a rule had everything to gain and nothing to

lose by trying very hard, wherein the children of today have so much given to them that their sense of values is rather distorted and they feel as though the world owes them a living. So, therefore, they don't try quite as hard.
